summary:
Rājasthān stands under India's national framework on gender identity, and no state-level deviation from that framework has been sourced. The Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Amendment Bill was passed by both houses of India's Parliament in March 2026 and awaits presidential assent, so the recognition rules a visitor encounters in this state are those of the amended national statute.

The amendment removes the right to self-identification that the 2019 Act had carried forward from the Supreme Court's 2014 third-gender judgment. Legal recognition is now limited to historically accepted socio-cultural groups such as hijra and kinner, and to intersex individuals. Trans men, trans women and non-binary people who self-identify outside those categories fall outside the recognition scheme entirely, and identity recognition is tied to medical certification rather than to the applicant's own declaration.

Human Rights Watch, writing on 26 March 2026, calls the amendment a major setback that strips thousands of people of rights and increases their exposure to harm. The government presents the change as widening access to welfare schemes and protection from trafficking; critics, including opposition parties and LGBTQ organisations that protested the bill, say it excludes many transgender, non-binary and gender-fluid people. India has an estimated two million transgender people.

For a trans visitor, the practical consequence sits in documents and in contact with officials. Identity-document practice now rests on medical certification under the amended scheme, and recognition remains uneven across the country, with continuing discrimination reported in education, healthcare and formal employment. The parent framework also documents exposure concentrated at checkpoints and in police contact: a trans woman alleged groping by a Railway Protection Force constable during a gender check at a railway station, transgender detainees described degrading treatment in Assam Railway Protection Force custody in interviews recorded in June 2024, CISF personnel stopped an openly transgender law student, Sakshi Jain, at Chennai International Airport Terminal 1 in November 2024 despite her PAN card, and passport authorities required a trans applicant to sit a medical examination before the Allahabad High Court granted relief in February 2026.

Criminal-law protection weakened in 2024. Replacing the Indian Penal Code with the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita removed the gender-identity-specific offences that had shielded trans people from sexual violence, and trans communities report fear of a rise in assaults under the new code. Same-sex acts were decriminalised by the Supreme Court in 2018 and discrimination is barred on grounds including sex, interpreted to cover gender identity, but same-sex marriage and civil partnership are not available, although courts have acknowledged same-sex couples as family units.
tangentialFactors:
The courts remain the strongest protection machinery against the narrowed statutory position. The Madras High Court's judgment of 7 June 2021 in S. Sushma v Commissioner of Police, delivered by Justice N. Anand Venkatesh, followed police harassment of a same-sex couple and issued sweeping guidelines covering police sensitisation, a ban on conversion therapy, and directions to the National Medical Commission and education authorities. The UK Home Office's country note of December 2025 records only limited reports of police abuse of LGBT+ people, likelier in conservative rural areas and not systemic.

The direction of travel runs against the 2014 Supreme Court ruling rather than alongside it: the court opened recognition on a self-identification basis, and the 2026 amendment narrows it to defined socio-cultural groups and intersex people. That reversal is the main turbulence in the current environment, and it is contested politically as well as legally, with opposition parties and LGBTQ groups protesting in March 2026 while the government frames the amendment as an expansion of welfare access.

Checkpoint friction is documented across modes of travel rather than confined to one state, which is why a visitor to Rājasthān should expect the same screening behaviour seen at railway stations, airports and passport offices elsewhere in India. The pattern is consistent: gender verification demanded at a security line, custody treatment predicated on gender presentation, and medical examination imposed as a condition of document issuance.
localsOnly:
Residents of Rājasthān are governed by the same amended national scheme as visitors, and for them the change bears directly on access to welfare schemes, identity documents and legal recognition. The government's stated purpose in passing the amendment was to make welfare benefits more accessible and to strengthen protection from trafficking, while the practical effect reported by critics is that transgender, non-binary and gender-fluid residents who do not belong to a historically recognised group or the intersex category are excluded from recognition altogether.

Medical certification is the gate to identity recognition for residents as well, replacing the self-declaration route that the 2019 Act had provided. Residents also continue to face discrimination in education, healthcare and formal employment, and recognition practice remains uneven across the country.

Domestic violence and sexual-assault protection is thinner than it was before 2024, because the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita dropped the gender-identity-specific offences of the Indian Penal Code. Residents who are detained by police or railway authorities face the custody conditions documented in 2024 interviews, and the protest activity of March 2026 indicates organised domestic opposition to the amendment rather than settled acceptance.
outOfScopeNotes:
Presidential assent to the Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Amendment Bill was still outstanding at the time of the March 2026 reporting, and whether it has since been assented to and brought into force is unresolved in the sources available here.

No Rājasthān-specific enforcement data has been sourced: there is no record in this inventory of how the state police, transport authorities or document offices in Rājasthān apply the amended recognition rules, and no Rājasthān case law on recognition, medical certification or checkpoint treatment is available to cite.

Whether Rājasthān's state welfare schemes have been re-drawn to follow the amended definition of transgender identity is not sourced. The inventory also does not establish how medical certification is operationalised in practice for a visitor applying for or renewing documents while in the state, nor whether the guidelines issued in the Madras High Court's 2021 judgment have any binding application outside that court's territory.
